name: Connecticut River Estuary
blurb: Tidal marsh, shad runs and ospreys where the river meets Long Island Sound.

tip.title: Cut the shad run
tip.text: Shad feed striped bass and harbor seals. Set American shad to -80% and watch the bass and seals. Shad numbers in the river fell by about 80% from 1992 to 2005.

notes: The species list comes from GBIF occurrence records inside a circle around the park, so it can include nearby areas. Feeding links come from GloBI records and the sources listed where they state them; others are general ecology and are illustrative.

nodes.desc: A common grazer of grasses and marsh plants along the river and shore.
Tiny grazers of phytoplankton. Young menhaden and shad feed on them.
A filter-feeding schooling fish. Striped bass, ospreys and eagles all prey on it.
An omnivorous marsh and estuary crab that preys on ribbed mussels.
Forages along the marsh edge, where it takes ribbed mussels among many other foods.
A shoreline generalist that eats shellfish and scavenges dead fish.
Spends its adult life mostly in salt water and enters rivers to spawn. Feeds on shad, river herring and menhaden.
Fish are about 99 percent of its diet. Nests on platforms and poles along the river and marsh.
Takes fish such as menhaden along the river and shore, and also eats carrion.
Hunts fish in Long Island Sound and has been recorded as far up the river as Holyoke, Massachusetts.
Twice a day the tide floods and uncovers the estuary marsh, setting when mussels and plankton can feed.
